text: Qq. ad Thalas. q. 61, παθούσης· quod et legendum.
anchorLine: πρὸς δὲ τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν τῆς ἀπαθοῦς * φύσεως (q),
en: The Questions to Thalassius, q. 61, has 'pathouses' (suffering) here; that too is what should be read. (The editor would read 'passible' for 'impassible'; a variant/conjecture on the word.)
note: the asterisk after ἀπαθοῦς is a small raised mark read as an asterisk at 600 dpi

text: Τῆς ἀπαθοῦς φύσεως. Sic dicta in Christo natura, sicque repræsentant codd. atque edita, cui proinde labor atque mors, ἄδικος ὁμοῦ καὶ ἀναίτιος foret. Sed mihi istud durius : longe vero expeditius ; quod habetur, Quæst. ad Thal. πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν τῆς παθούσης φύσεως : quod et reddidi. Sic certe tota laborabat natura, totaque reparanda, Christi laboribus et morte non naturæ ἀπαθοῦς, quod nec ipsa sic absolute dicatur Christi natura, quæ τὸ παθητὸν carnis haberet, quantumvis esset ἀπαθής, quod ad vitium attinet ac culpam.
anchorLine: πρὸς δὲ τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν τῆς ἀπαθοῦς * φύσεως (q),
en: 'Of the impassible nature.' The editor says the nature in Christ is so called, and so the manuscripts and the printed texts have it, which would make labour and death at once unjust and without cause for it. But to him that is rather harsh; far easier is what stands in the Questions to Thalassius, 'for the correction of the suffering nature', which he has also rendered so. In that way indeed the whole nature was labouring and wholly to be repaired by Christ's labours and death, not a nature 'impassible', since the nature of Christ is not said to be so absolutely, as it had the passible element of flesh, even though it was impassible as regards vice and guilt.
